questions.q: What is the main practical difference between hierarchical clustering and k-means?
options: Hierarchical clustering builds a full tree of merges, and you choose the number of clusters afterward by cutting it
Hierarchical clustering only works on two features
k-means produces a dendrogram; hierarchical clustering does not
questions.explain: Agglomerative clustering records every merge in a tree, and you pick where to cut it, rather than committing to k up front.

questions.q: With 300 rows, how many merges does agglomerative clustering perform to reach a single cluster?
questions.explain: Each merge reduces the cluster count by one, so going from 300 clusters to 1 takes 299 merges, matching the (299, 4) shape of the linkage table.

questions.q: The last three merge distances in the ward linkage were 4.31, 22.46, and 24.31. What does the jump from 4.31 to 22.46 suggest?
options: Cutting just before that jump gives three natural groups
questions.explain: A large jump means two very different groups were merged. Cutting the tree below it leaves three well-separated clusters.

questions.q: Which linkage did the lesson use to split two interlocking crescents correctly (150 and 150)?
questions.explain: Single linkage merges by the closest pair of members, so it can follow a curved chain. Ward gave 184 and 116, cutting across the crescents.

questions.q: Why is hierarchical clustering a poor choice for millions of rows?
options: It compares many pairs of rows, so time and memory grow quickly with dataset size
questions.explain: The pairwise comparisons make it comfortable for thousands of rows but very expensive for millions, where k-means scales better.
